newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Strengthening of Colombian oil sector alarms group.
newsitem.headline: Strengthening of Colombian oil sector alarms group.

text.p: A leading financial group voiced alarm over Colombia's fledgling oil boom Monday, saying it could soon turn to bust with the country drowning in a flood of petrodollars.

The warning came from the prestigious National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF), which said an influx of dollars from foreign oil sales were already lending artificial support to Colombia's buoyant peso.

This, in turn, has made Colombian exports less competitive abroad and contributed to "the contraction of industry, agriculture, coffee and lesser exports as a result of the growth of the oil sector," the ANIF said in a weekly report on the economy.

The peso, which was trading at 1,070 in late June, has risen steadily in recent weeks and closed at a seven-month high of 1,022.00 last Thursday, a day after President Ernesto Samper announced what he described as a major new oil find in the country's eastern plains.

The government had forecast a 13.6 percent devaluation of the peso this year. But the currency has lost less than 5.0 percent of its value against the dollar so far, and the ANIF report said this had left many exporters in "the initial phases of panic" as their goods become less competitive in the global marketplace.
The central bank, which likes a strong peso as a buffer against inflation, has insisted that it will not alter its floating exchange rate band in a bid to undercut the peso artificially.

But ANIF said in its report that "the growing crisis among exporters" was likely to step up pressure on the central bank to either devalue the peso outright or weaken it by buying dollars in the country's foreign exchange market.
Samper himself has appealed to the central bank's board of directors to devalue the peso to help jump-start the economy, which has slowed considerably this year.
But Samper has little control over the board, with just two of its seven members -- including Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo -- considered among his loyalists.
The situation could change next Februrary, however, when the terms of two board members expire and Samper will have a free hand to nominate new members.
